title: Samech
hook: the round letter of support, samach, to lean on

segments.voice: Yesterday, nun and samech, the gap in Ashrei. Your line was nun falls, samech lifts. Did you reach the person who stumbled? Today, samech gets a day of its own. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

Moses is near the end, and he asks God for a successor, someone to go out before the people so they won't be like sheep with no shepherd. God names Joshua, and gives Moses an instruction. Take him, and lay your hand on him. Hand, singular. In Hebrew the word is yadecha, your hand. A few verses later the text tells us what Moses actually did. In the King James words: "And he laid his hands upon him." Hands. Plural. Both of them. He was asked for one and gave two. Today's letter is the one that names that gesture.
screen: `MOSES ASKS FOR A SUCCESSOR.` → `LAY YOUR HAND ON HIM.` → `HE LAID BOTH HANDS.`

segments.voice: Samech. On the page it's nearly a closed circle. Its sound is a plain s, and its root, samach, means to lean on, to rest your weight against something. Turn it four ways. First, the hands. When Moses lays his hands on Joshua, the verb is vayismoch, from that same root. He isn't patting him on the head. He's leaning on him, putting his own weight on the younger man's shoulders, as if to say: what held me up now rests on you. The medieval commentator Rashi notices the change from one hand to two and says Moses did it generously, more than he was asked. Second, a name. Rabbinic ordination is still called semichah, the same word: a teacher's authority, leaned onto a student. Third, the Temple. In Leviticus, a person bringing an offering lays a hand on the animal's head before it is offered. Same verb again. Some readers hear it this way: before you give something up, you lean on it, you make it yours. Fourth, the shape. Some teachers read samech's closed circle as a picture of support with no gap in it, a ring that holds whatever is inside. Yesterday, samech was the verse that catches the one who fell. Today it's the hand on a shoulder before anyone falls at all. Support, in Hebrew, isn't only rescue. It's leaning in early, with both hands, and letting someone feel the weight of your trust.
screen: `SAMACH: TO LEAN ON.` · `MOSES LEANS ON JOSHUA.` · `SEMICHAH: HANDS THAT PASS IT ON.` · `A ROUND LETTER WITH NO GAP.` · then, large: `AND HE LAID HIS HANDS UPON HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: support someone. Settle, and breathe. Feel what's holding you up right now: the chair, the floor, the wall at your back. Lean into it a little and notice it doesn't move. Then bring to mind someone who is carrying something new. A first job, a new baby, a new role, a hard diagnosis. Ask what both hands would look like for them, not just one. An hour of your time, a question you actually wait to hear answered. If you pray, you can hold them in it. The bell holds the time.
Samech. The round letter whose root means to lean on, the root of semichah, the laying on of hands. Today's word.
Your line: samech supports. Today, give the one you thought of more than they asked for: both hands, not one. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Rabbinic ordination is called semichah, after Moses laying his hands on Joshua; Jewish students learn samech as the letter of the root meaning to lean on or support.

fork.setup: you're Moses. God names Joshua as the next leader and tells you to lay your hand on him. what do you do?
options: lay one hand, exactly as told.
send Joshua to the priest instead.
fork.reveal: "and he laid his hands upon him": both hands. Rashi reads it as Moses giving more than he was asked.

original.note: Hebrew: leaning, laying on of hands — the word for rabbinic ordination.

trapdoor: what you thought: samech is just an s sound.
what it means: its root, samach, means to lean on: Moses leans both hands on Joshua to pass on his role.
what a scholar hears: Numbers 27:18 says yadecha, your hand; 27:23 says yadav, his hands. Rashi reads the change as generosity.

sources.quoted: And he laid his hands upon him

notes: Numbers 27:23 fragment quoted from KJV; JPS 1917 has the same words for this fragment, I believe. Confirm.
Samech described only as 'nearly a closed circle'.
Rashi on 27:23 (Moses laid both hands, generously, 'b'ayin yafah') paraphrased. Confirm.

Semichah as the name of rabbinic ordination, and its link to Moses and Joshua, is standard; confirm phrasing 'still ordained with a ceremony called semichah' (modern semichah is usually a certificate rather than a physical laying on of hands).
The reading of samech's closed shape as support is homiletic, attributed to 'some teachers'. Confirm or cut.
